items.name: part1
items.direction: Narrate this as a popular geography YouTube channel's long-form explainer. The Narrator is a deep, warm, confident storyteller: curious and brisk, with natural emphasis, building wonder as we go deeper, a short comic pause before each punchline, and real awe at the big reveals. Chars voices funny cartoon characters: short and punchy. Read numbers naturally.
lines: Narrator
Start digging in Delhi and never stop. Twelve thousand kilometres later... where do you come out?
Narrator
The planet will try to stop you four times. And humans have tried. We got about 0.2 percent of the way.
Narrator
So let's go further than anyone ever has. Starting with the deepest hole on Earth.
Narrator
Rewind to 1970. Far north in Russia, near the border with Norway, Soviet scientists start drilling. Straight down.
Narrator
The hole is narrower than a dinner plate. About 23 centimetres. And they keep going... for 19 years.
Narrator
By 1989, it reaches 12,262 metres. Drop Mount Everest in, and it would vanish. It's even deeper than the Mariana Trench.
Narrator
But down there, it was about 180 degrees. Nearly double what they'd expected.
Narrator
And the rock stopped behaving like rock. It turned soft, like hot plastic, and crept back into the hole.
Narrator
So in the early nineties, they stopped. Today, the deepest hole on Earth is a rusty metal cap... in an abandoned field.
Chars
[tired, grumpy old metal lid, deadpan] Deepest hole on Earth. Please stop sitting on me.
Narrator
And the twist? After 19 years... they only got about a third of the way through the crust.
Narrator
So if our best drill gave up at 12 kilometres... how do we know what's 6,000 kilometres down?
Narrator
Let's cheat. Imagine a drill pod that can't melt. Back to Delhi... and down we go.
Narrator
First, the crust. Under the oceans, it's only about 5 to 10 kilometres thick. Under the continents, around 30 to 50.
Narrator
Shrink the Earth to the size of an apple, and the crust is thinner than its skin.
Narrator
And it heats up fast. Every kilometre down adds about 25 to 30 degrees.
Narrator
The deepest mine on Earth, in South Africa, goes about 4 kilometres down. The rock there hits about 60 degrees. Miners need huge cooling systems just to work.

items.direction: Narrate this as a popular geography YouTube channel's long-form explainer. lines: Narrator
Then, a few dozen kilometres down, earthquake waves suddenly speed up. A Croatian scientist spotted this in 1909. His name? Moho-ro-VEE-chich.
Narrator
So everyone just calls it... the Moho.
Narrator
Welcome to the mantle. About 2,900 kilometres thick. That's like Delhi to Bangkok... straight down.
Narrator
It's about 84 percent of the planet's volume. And it's solid rock... that slowly flows.
Narrator
That slow churn helps drag the plates above, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Chars
[slow, sleepy, deep and proud] I'm not lazy. I'm moving continents.
Narrator
India is still pushing into Asia, a few centimetres a year. That's why the Himalayas are still rising.
Narrator
Down here it's over 1,000 degrees at the top, and nearly 4,000 at the bottom. The squeeze? More than a million times the air pressure on your skin.
Narrator
Then the rock just... ends. And we hit an ocean. Of liquid metal.
Narrator
The outer core. Mostly molten iron and nickel, about 2,200 kilometres deep, and roughly 4,500 to 5,500 degrees.
Narrator
And it's churning. That moving metal works like a giant dynamo... and makes Earth's magnetic field.
Narrator
That field shields us from the solar wind. It lights up the auroras. And it gives your compass a north to point at.
Narrator
So every compass on Earth... depends on a metal ocean you will never see.
Narrator
Keep going, and the liquid ends too. At the very centre, about 5,150 kilometres down... a solid ball.
Narrator
The inner core. Iron and nickel, with a radius of about 1,220 kilometres. Roughly 70 percent of the Moon's.
Narrator
It's somewhere around 5,200 to 6,000 degrees. About as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Narrator
So why isn't it melting? Pressure. Over 3 million times what you feel up here squeezes it solid.
Chars
[smug, fiery, show-off] Hotter than the Sun's surface. Still solid. You're welcome.

lines: Narrator
And it might be drifting. Recent studies suggest that since around 2010, it's been turning a little slower than the surface.
Narrator
Okay. Nobody has ever been anywhere near here. So how do we know any of this?
Narrator
Earthquakes. Every big quake sends waves through the whole planet. Seismographs on the other side catch them, like an X-ray of the Earth.
Narrator
One kind of wave can't cross liquid. So past a certain point, it never arrives. That shadow gave away the liquid outer core.
Narrator
Then in 1936, Danish seismologist Inge Lay-mun spotted faint waves bouncing where none should be. A core... inside the core.
Narrator
Her paper had one of the shortest titles in science. Just P, with a little dash.
Narrator
There's a backup clue too. The whole planet is about twice as dense as its surface rocks. So the middle must be heavy metal.
Narrator
So. Imagine our hole goes all the way through... and you jump in.
Narrator
You'd fall faster and faster, hitting about 28,000 kilometres an hour at the centre. For a moment... you'd float.
Narrator
Then gravity slows you down, and about 40 minutes later, you reach the other side. Shorter than a Delhi traffic jam.
Narrator
So... where do you come out? Not China. Not America.
Narrator
The exact opposite of Delhi is the South Pacific, about 3,000 kilometres off Chile. The nearest land? A tiny island about 350 kilometres away... with nobody on it.
Narrator
And that's normal. Most of the world's land sits opposite ocean. Dig almost anywhere... and you come up wet.
Chars
[squeaky, indignant, cheeky little fish] Twelve thousand kilometres... and no swimsuit?
Narrator
Six thousand kilometres of rock, metal and fire. And we still haven't drilled past the first twelve.
Narrator
This is Bhoogol. Follow for more Geography Fun Facts.
